newsitem.title: USA: Brazil Sao Paulo to start privatizing by 1998.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Sao Paulo to start privatizing by 1998.

text.p: Brazil's industrial powerhouse of Sao Paulo state will start the privatization of its multibillion dollar electrical holdings at the end of the year, the state's energy secretary said on Monday.

The official, David Zylbersztajn, told potential investors that consultants would be hired next month to recommend minimum prices and the system for selling the government's share of the three major state power companies -- distributor Companhia Paulista De Forca e Luz, or CPFL; generator Companhia Energetica De Sao Paulo, or Cesp; and distributor Electropaulo.
"We expect sales to start this November or December," Zylbersztajn told potential investors at a conference.
"There will be a final decision by the governor on the form of payment and how they can be sold."
He said CPFL would be the first company sold, likely followed by CESP's distribution arm. He added that the timetable remained flexible.
"These companies all go together, it depends on the consultants and the state of the market. But now, it's CPFL first," he told Reuters.
The sale of the companies will be among the biggest in Latin American history. Some examples of their size:
* The three companies have a net worth of $18 billion;.
*They have 15 percent of all installed capacity in Latin America, or 11.8 gigawatts;
*Their annual billings equal those of Consolidated Edison Co of New York.
Executives for the companies say they have been cutting costs and slashing bloated payrolls to prepare for the sales.
For example, CESP cut its staff to 10,900 as of last month from 19,700 in December 1994. Electropaulo cut the number of unmetered connections to zero at the end of 1996 from 64,000 in December 1995.

Sao Paulo officials said energy use was forecast to grow an average of 4.3 percent a year from 1997 to 2006, against an annual increase in gross domestic product of four percent through 2001, and five percent form 2001 to 2006. They also forecast a 10 percent to 12 percent increase in electrical rates, most of which will take place after the sales go through.

Under the laws governing privatization, the state government will keep 51 percent of the voting shares in transmission. The number of companies that can be created by the possible breakup of CPFL, CESP and Electropaulo is limited to 20.
Penn Cox, South America projects director for Duke Power Co, said the potential growth of energy needs made the Sau Paulo companies attractive.
"They are both attractive and daunting at the same time because of their size," he said. "They are kind of on the scale of the Australian companies that were privatized."
